name: Carrot maxxing

lead: Carrot maxxing means eating lots of carrots or similar foods to give the skin a golden or orange tone without sun. The effect it relies on, carotenemia, is real and documented.

The chain is dietary: carotenoids from food accumulate in the outer skin layer and tint it. According to Wikipedia, colour typically appears after several weeks of high intake and fades over months after stopping. The medical literature on carotenemia consists of case descriptions and reviews focused on telling it apart from jaundice; no trials have tested it as a cosmetic method.

paras: People eat carotenoid-rich foods such as carrots, sweet potato and similar produce in large amounts daily, sometimes as juice. The tint builds gradually over weeks, often most visible on palms and soles and in the face, and it fades slowly once intake drops.

Carotenemia is generally described as benign, but it can mimic jaundice, and orange skin has been associated with conditions such as hypothyroidism and eating disorders. A report described amenorrhea in women with diet-induced carotenemia.

chain: Carotenoids build up in outer skin
angle.text: You eat large amounts of carrots and other carotenoid-rich foods so carotenoids build up in the outer skin and give a golden glow without sun exposure. The tint builds over weeks. Carotenemia is a documented, benign condition described in the medical literature.

lead: Carrot maxxing is the looksmaxxing practice of eating large amounts of carrots or other carotenoid-rich foods to give the skin a golden or orange tint. It relies on carotenemia (also called carotenosis or carotenoderma), a documented, benign condition in which excess dietary carotenoids accumulate in the outer skin layer [1][2].

Practitioners pursue it as a food-based way to warm the complexion: a sun-kissed look without UV exposure, or a healthier-looking glow that stands out against pale or sallow skin. Psychology research has examined the idea behind it. Psychology studies have asked whether carotenoid-based yellowness is attractive, with titles including 'Fruit over sunbed: carotenoid skin colouration is found more attractive than melanin colouration' (2015) and a cross-cultural study reporting that carotenoid colouration enhances face and body attractiveness (2019) [3].

Medical literature on carotenemia itself is mostly clinical: case descriptions, reviews and differential diagnosis, with emphasis on telling it apart from jaundice [1][2]. No clinical studies have tested it as a cosmetic technique, and looksmax.org members have posted mixed results from attempting it [4].

paras: The method is dietary. Practitioners eat carrots or other carotenoid-rich foods in quantity, and carotenoids deposit in the skin gradually. Wikipedia lists carrots, sweet potatoes, squash, pumpkins, spinach, apricots and tomatoes among foods rich in carotenoids, with tomatoes the main source of lycopene [1]. Its appeal to looksmaxxers is as a no-UV alternative to tanning, using only food.

Wikipedia describes carotenosis as a harmless, reversible orange discolouration of the skin due to excess carotenoids, most visible in light-skinned people and often most noticeable on palms, soles, knees and nasolabial folds; it spares the whites of the eyes, which helps distinguish it from jaundice [1]. Intake above roughly 20 mg per day is described as likely to cause it, while the average US adult takes in about 2.3 mg per day and one medium carrot contains about 4.0 mg; colour takes about four to seven weeks to be clinically recognised [1]. A related condition from lycopene, lycopenemia, was described in a 1960 New England Journal of Medicine report and shows as deep orange skin with discolouration of the soft palate [1][5].

Medical reviews note that carrots and other yellow vegetables are the usual cause and that the condition matters mainly because it can be confused with jaundice [2]. A 1958 report in the Annals of Internal Medicine collected observations on carotenemia [6].

Carotenoids are absorbed passively from the gut, partly converted to vitamin A in the intestinal lining and liver, and carried in plasma to tissues; they leave through sweat, sebum, urine and gut secretions, and deposit in the intercellular lipids of the stratum corneum, which is why colour is strongest where that layer is thick or sweating is high [1]. Processed and pureed foods make carotene more available for absorption, which is why infants on mashed vegetables are prone to it [1]. In more darkly pigmented people it may show chiefly on the palms and soles, and it is easier to see under artificial light [1]. Primary carotenoderma comes from diet or supplements, while secondary forms come from underlying disease, and the two can coexist [1].

Psychologists have studied carotenoid skin colour as a candidate health signal. PubMed lists about 28 papers on the topic, including a 2012 review by Whitehead, Ozakinci and Perrett on harnessing the attractiveness of skin coloration to improve diet and health [3]. The 2015 study by Lefevre and Perrett, titled 'Fruit over sunbed', reports that carotenoid colouration was found more attractive than melanin colouration, and describes skin yellowness as shaped by both dietary carotenoids and melanin. A 2019 cross-cultural study by Ip, Lewis and Lefevre reported that faces with more carotenoid colouration were perceived as healthier and that colouration enhanced face and body attractiveness [3].

A 2013 study by Lefevre and colleagues, 'It is all in the face', reported that carotenoid skin colouration loses its attractiveness advantage outside the face. Researchers present carotenoid colour as a possible signal of fruit and vegetable intake, and the work concerns perception, not a recommended practice.
Proponents say a carotenoid tint reads as healthier or more attractive than pale skin and can substitute for tanning, and they point to the perception studies above.

One looksmax.org thread asks whether anyone has deliberately gotten a carotenemia tan and whether it is worthwhile. The original poster reported eating about thirty two-pound bags of carrots without any visible tan [4]. This matches the clinical description that timing and visibility vary and depend on skin tone and the amount absorbed [1].

Carotenemia also occurs with some diseases. Wikipedia lists hypothyroidism, diabetes mellitus, restricting anorexia nervosa, nephrotic syndrome, kidney dysfunction and liver disease as secondary causes, and describes impaired conversion to retinol and raised blood lipids as mechanisms in some [1][7]. A 1983 JAMA report described ten women with anovulation, nine with amenorrhea, who had diet-induced carotenemia and ate pure or predominantly vegetarian diets [8]. The report does not establish that carotenemia itself is the cause. Wikipedia states that carotenosis itself is generally considered harmless and typically fades over several months after high intake stops [1].

No studies found on carrot maxxing as a cosmetic practice. Clinical literature on carotenemia exists, consisting of case reports and reviews focused on diagnosis [2][6]. Related perception experiments on carotenoid colour and attractiveness are described above [3].

Carotenemia is described as harmless and reversible [1]. The main practical issue is confusion with jaundice: carotenemia spares the whites of the eyes, which helps clinicians distinguish them, and Wikipedia also contrasts it with argyria and chrysiasis, which cause blue-grey skin and are irreversible [1][2]. Because carotenemia accompanies hypothyroidism, diabetes, anorexia nervosa and other conditions, orange skin can prompt medical evaluation [1][7]. A 1983 JAMA series linked diet-induced carotenemia with amenorrhea in women on vegetarian diets [8].

Wikipedia notes that canthaxanthin, a food colouring used in US and European 'tanning pills', is not FDA-approved for that purpose and has been linked to hepatitis, urticaria, aplastic anemia and retinopathy with visual field defects, which is a different compound and a different risk from food carotenoids [1]. High-dose beta-carotene is prescribed for erythropoietic protoporphyria and has been found harmless though cosmetically displeasing to some [1].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org carrot maxxing is discussed as a cheap, food-only way to get a golden tone, with some members reporting no visible effect [4].

claims.claim: Eating lots of carrots gives a golden, healthy-looking tan.
A carotenoid tint is more attractive than a sun tan.
It works for everyone who eats enough carrots.
The orange colour is entirely harmless.
Tanning pills are an equivalent shortcut.
